extracted.intended_audience: marketing researchers, practitioners, and designers of online content interested in factors driving virality
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and predicting what characteristics of online articles drive social transmission (virality), focusing on emotional content, practical value, placement, and other content and author features. Uses NYT archival data and experiments to identify measurable predictors of making the NYT "most e-mailed" list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity (Valence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which an article is positive versus negative (valence). Quantified as the difference between the percentage of positive and negative words in an article (LIWC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More positive content is more likely to be shared; positivity has a larger positive association with making the most-e-mailed list than negative-word percentage. Results persist controlling for other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotionality (Affect-ladenness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall affect-ladenness measured as the percentage of words classified as either positive or negative (LIWC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More affect-laden (emotional) content, regardless of valence, is more likely to become viral; emotionality is a positive predictor of making the most-e-mailed list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awe (high-arousal positive emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which content evokes awe — defined as a feeling of admiration/elevation in the face of something greater than the self (manually coded, 1–5 Likert averaged across 3 raters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awe (a high-arousal positive emotion) is positively associated with virality; a one-standard-deviation increase in awe substantially raises odds of making the most-e-mailed list (~30%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger (high-arousal negative emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which content evokes anger (manually coded, 1–5 Likert averaged across 3 raters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anger (a high-arousal negative emotion) is positively associated with virality; increases in anger meaningfully increase the odds of making the most-e-mailed list (~34% per 1 SD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anxiety (high-arousal negative emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which content evokes anxiety (manually coded, 1–5 Likert averaged across 3 raters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anxiety (a high-arousal negative emotion) is positively associated with virality; anxiety-inducing stories are more likely to be shared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sadness (low-arousal negative emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which content evokes sadness (manually coded, 1–5 Likert averaged across 3 raters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sadness (a low-arousal/deactivating negative emotion) is negatively associated with virality; sadder content is less likely to be shared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disgust (negative emotion control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which content evokes disgust (manually coded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a control because prior work linked disgust to transmission; in this data set disgust had no significant relationship with virality (no effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical utility (usefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which an article contains practically useful information that could change behavior (manually coded, 1–5 Likert).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically useful content is more likely to be shared; practical value is a significant positive predictor of making the most-e-mailed list and is controlled for in models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which an article is interesting (manually coded, 1–5 Likert).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More interesting articles are more likely to be shared; interest is a positive control variable in analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which an article evokes surprise (manually coded, 1–5 Likert).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprising content is more likely to be shared; surprise is included as a control and positively relates to virality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home page placement and exposure time
rubrics_metrics.description: Where on the NYT home page an article appears and how long it spends in each of seven aggregated regions (captured by web crawler; hours spent per region).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominent placement and longer exposure (especially lead/top feature time) strongly increase the probability of making the most-e-mailed list; models control for placement and Winsorize top 1% outliers on exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance in physical newspaper (section and page)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which section (e.g., A) and page (e.g., A1) an article appears in the physical paper (captured by crawler).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as control variables to account for offline prominence and its potential impact on online sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release timing (time of day) and day dummies
rubrics_metrics.description: Time of day when the article first appeared online (6 A.M.–6 P.M. or 6 P.M.–6 A.M. Eastern) and day fixed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controls for temporal effects that might influence attention and sharing; models include day fixed effects and time-of-day controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author fame
rubrics_metrics.description: Proxy for author prominence measured as the (log of) number of Google hits returned for the first author's full name (captured Feb 15, 2009).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More famous authors' articles are more likely to be shared; include as a control to ensure results not driven by popular writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing complexity (SMOG Complexity Index)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readability/complexity measured via the SMOG Complexity Index (grade-level appropriateness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a control; alternate complexity measures yield similar results. Models control for complexity when assessing emotion effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count / Article length
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of article measured in words (captured by crawler).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer articles are more likely to be shared (may evoke more emotion or contain more information); included as a control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author gender
rubrics_metrics.description: First-author gender coded (male/female/unknown) using a name-to-gender mapping and online lookup for ambiguous cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles by women were found more likely to make the most-e-mailed list; gender is included as a control (with 'unknown' dummy if missing byline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent variable: Making the NYT "most e-mailed" list (binary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary outcome: whether an article ever earned a position on the New York Times' 24-hour most e-mailed list (binary: 1 = made list at least once, 0 = never).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistic regression (primary specification) models this binary outcome with day fixed effects and clustered standard errors by day; used to identify predictors of virality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative outcomes: Highest rank and hours on list
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancillary dependent measures: the highest rank achieved on the most-e-mailed list (ordered/ranked) and the number of hours an article spent on the list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordered logit used for rank (with never-on-list coded as 26); OLS used for hours on list. Both yield consistent patterns but have selection/interpretation caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated sentiment measurement (LIWC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of LIWC to count positive and negative words from a 7,630-word human-classified lexicon; positivity and emotionality derived from these counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated sentiment increases coding ease and objectivity; automated ratings significantly correlate with manual coder ratings. Positivity = %positive − %negative; emotionality = %positive_or_negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual coding procedure for specific emotions and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Human coders rated awe, anger, anxiety, sadness, surprise, practical utility, and interest on 1–5 Likert scales using title, summary, and link to full text; three independent raters per dimension; interrater reliability α > .70; scores averaged and standardized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coders were blind to hypotheses and trained with feedback on a test set. A random subsample (n = 2566) was hand-coded due to dataset size; uncoded articles assigned mean (0 after standardization) with a dummy in regressions to control for imputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputation and handling of uncoded articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncoded articles were assigned a score of zero after standardization (equivalent to the mean), and a dummy variable indicating uncoded status was included in regressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard imputation methodology (Cohen & Cohen 1983); results are similar when analyzing only the hand-coded subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling choices and robustness practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary specification: logistic regression predicting making the list with day fixed effects and standard errors clustered by day. Controls included for content, placement, author, timing, and topic; various robustness checks performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robustness checks include ordered logit for rank, OLS for hours on list, Winsorizing top/bottom 1% of outliers, adding squared/cubed terms for exposure, splitting exposure by day/night, including topic dummies, testing interactions, removing fixed effects — findings remain consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical mechanism: Activation / Arousal dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis that level of physiological arousal (activation) evoked by content drives sharing behavior independent of valence: high-arousal emotions mobilize action (sharing), low-arousal emotions inhibit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predicts and explains empirical pattern: high-arousal emotions (awe, anger, anxiety) increase virality regardless of valence; low-arousal (sadness) decreases virality. Use arousal as a design criterion beyond simple positive/negative valence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding definitions (construct clarification for coders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational definitions provided to coders for emotions and control constructs (anger, anxiety, awe, sadness, surprise, practical utility, interest) with links to reference definitions and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coders were instructed to rate articles by how much each construct would evoke in typical readers, provided example anchors and training feedback until understanding was acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home page region aggregation (seven-region scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregation of dozens of exact home page positions into seven general regions that receive similar attention; time spent in each region used as control variables (hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregation simplifies positional controls; the home page layout was stable during collection. Analyses Winsorize extreme exposure values and include alternative specifications (dummies for ever appearing in a region, or separate day/night exposure).
